h.select_rule: Keep hypotheses whose direction goes against the first intuitive guess but which a reported empirical regularity or a general statistical effect (headroom, floor, saturation, redundancy) supports. Drop those with rare conditions or tiny expected effects. Keep variety across edited fields.
h.strategy: Use the retrieved literature to find measured interaction patterns, not design advice: reports that an option's benefit shrinks, vanishes or reverses depending on what else is present, or that strong configurations respond differently from weak ones. Translate each reported pattern into a conditional hypothesis about this benchmark. Write queries about interactions, diminishing returns and context-dependent effects among components. Include hypotheses in which strong parents gain less from improvements and lose more from degradations. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy.

hyps.why: A conv already feeding the output from node 1 gives diminishing returns for another conv on the direct edge.
When the direct output edge is already a strong conv, extra conv capacity on edge 1 adds less.
A strong first edge leaves less headroom for an internal conv upgrade.
Redundant strong convs into the output give diminishing returns.
Another conv into the output adds less when the direct edge is already a strong conv.
A conv on edge 1 gives an alternative input path, so removing edge 0 costs less.
With the node-2 path to the output cut, the direct 0->3 edge carries more of the output signal, so upgrading it matters more.
Replacing a missing edge with a conv gains more than replacing an op that already passes signal.
Giving the output a direct path where there was none yields a larger gain than replacing an existing op.
Restoring a cut output edge with a conv gives a larger gain than swapping one working op for another.
